fermat-little.name: Fermat's little theorem
fermat-little.oneLiner: The theorem guaranteeing that for a prime p and an integer a coprime to it, a to the (p-1)th power leaves remainder 1 on division by p
fermat-little.description: Fermat's little theorem says that when a prime p does not divide a, the remainder of a^(p-1) on division by p is always 1. It simplifies modular exponentiation dramatically, and it forms the theoretical foundation of the RSA cryptosystem.
fermat-little.significance: It is a cornerstone of modern cryptography, and it is essential to primality testing algorithms and to computing modular inverses.

a.description: An integer coprime to the prime p. It is the base of the power.

p.description: The prime that the division is taken with respect to.

p-1.description: One less than the prime; raising to this power leaves a remainder of 1.

\\equiv 1.description: It says the result of the modular operation is 1.

realWorldExamples: Computing modular inverses of large numbers in the RSA cryptosystem
Screening prime candidates in a primality test (the Fermat test)
Analyzing collision probabilities when designing a hash function

euler-theorem.name: Euler's theorem
euler-theorem.oneLiner: The theorem that for coprime integers a and n, a raised to Euler's totient of n leaves remainder 1 on division by n
euler-theorem.description: Euler's theorem extends Fermat's little theorem to composite numbers. When a and n are coprime, raising a to the power of Euler's totient function leaves a remainder of 1 on division by n. Fermat's little theorem is the special case where n is prime.
euler-theorem.significance: As the generalization of Fermat's little theorem it is used directly to prove that RSA works, and it provides the basis for modular arithmetic with composite moduli.

n.description: The positive integer that the division is taken with respect to.

\\varphi(n).description: How many integers from 1 to n are coprime to n.

\\equiv 1.description: It says the result of the modular operation is 1.

realWorldExamples: The mathematical basis for computing the decryption exponent in RSA
Analyzing the security of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol
Computing the order of a cyclic group

prime-counting.name: Prime number theorem
prime-counting.oneLiner: The theorem showing that the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x/ln(x)
prime-counting.description: The prime number theorem shows that, for large enough x, the function counting the primes up to x converges to x/ln(x). It proves the striking fact that although the distribution of primes looks irregular, at large scale it follows a predictable density.
prime-counting.discoverer: Jacques Hadamard, Charles de la Vallée Poussin (independent proofs)
prime-counting.significance: It is the most basic theorem about the distribution of primes, and the starting point of analytic number theory, tied directly to the Riemann hypothesis.

\\pi(x).description: The function counting how many primes there are up to x.

x.description: The upper end of the range over which primes are counted.

\\ln(x).description: The natural logarithm of x. It gives the rate at which prime density falls off.

\\sim.description: It means the ratio of the two functions converges to 1 as x grows without bound.

realWorldExamples: Estimating the search range when hunting for large primes for cryptography
Designing probabilistic primality tests using prime density
Statistical analysis of prime gaps in mathematical research

euclidean-algorithm.name: Euclidean algorithm
euclidean-algorithm.oneLiner: The algorithm that finds the greatest common divisor of two integers by repeatedly taking remainders
euclidean-algorithm.description: The Euclidean algorithm applies the property gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b) over and over to compute the greatest common divisor efficiently. The divisor at the moment the remainder hits 0 is the greatest common divisor. It is known as the oldest algorithm on record.
euclidean-algorithm.significance: It is the first algorithm ever recorded, and it is used throughout computer science — reducing fractions, computing modular inverses, generating RSA keys.

a.description: One of the two numbers whose greatest common divisor is wanted.

b.description: The other of the two numbers whose greatest common divisor is wanted.

\\gcd.description: The function returning the greatest common divisor of two integers.

a \\mod b.description: The remainder of a divided by b. You repeat until this value is 0.

realWorldExamples: Finding the greatest common divisor of numerator and denominator when reducing a fraction to lowest terms
Deriving the private key in RSA key generation with the extended Euclidean algorithm
Finding when two rhythmic cycles in music line up again, via their least common multiple

quadratic-reciprocity.name: Quadratic reciprocity
quadratic-reciprocity.oneLiner: The law showing that for two odd primes p and q, the quadratic residue relations settle each other symmetrically
quadratic-reciprocity.description: Quadratic reciprocity gives the exact relationship, for odd primes p and q, between whether p is a quadratic residue modulo q and whether q is a quadratic residue modulo p. Gauss called it the 'gem of arithmetic', and it was the first result to reveal a reciprocity principle in number theory.
quadratic-reciprocity.significance: It is the starting point of algebraic number theory and class field theory, and the key tool for deciding whether a quadratic equation has solutions modulo a prime.

p.description: One of the two primes the reciprocity law is applied to.

q.description: The other of the two primes the reciprocity law is applied to.

\\left(\\frac{p}{q}\\right).description: The symbol returning 1 if p is a quadratic residue modulo q and -1 otherwise.

(-1)^{\\frac{p-1}{2}\\cdot\\frac{q-1}{2}.description: The term that settles the sign of the product of the two Legendre symbols.

realWorldExamples: Quickly deciding whether a quadratic congruence has a solution
Designing cryptosystems based on quadratic residues
Generalizing to higher reciprocity laws in algebraic number theory research

goldbach-conjecture.name: Goldbach's conjecture
goldbach-conjecture.oneLiner: The unsolved conjecture that every even number greater than 2 can be written as the sum of two primes
goldbach-conjecture.description: Goldbach's conjecture claims that every even number from 4 up can be expressed as a sum of two primes. Goldbach first raised it in a 1742 letter to Euler; it has been verified by computer over an enormous range but never proved, which makes it one of the best-known open problems in mathematics.
goldbach-conjecture.significance: It is the archetypal hard problem of additive number theory, and it demands a deep understanding of how primes behave under addition.

p.description: One of the two primes making up the even number.

q.description: The other of the two primes making up the even number.

realWorldExamples: Large-scale numerical verification projects run by computer
Motivating additive problems in research on the distribution of primes
The standard example used in teaching to explain the difference between a conjecture and a proof

fibonacci-general.name: Binet's formula
fibonacci-general.oneLiner: The closed formula that computes the nth Fibonacci number directly from the golden ratio
fibonacci-general.description: Binet's formula computes the nth term of the Fibonacci sequence directly, without recursion, using the golden ratio and its conjugate. It is striking that a combination of irrational numbers always comes out to an integer, and it is the standard illustration of solving a linear recurrence through its characteristic equation.
fibonacci-general.discoverer: Jacques Philippe Marie Binet (formulation), Abraham de Moivre (earlier discovery)
fibonacci-general.significance: It shows that a linear recurrence can be solved in closed form, and it reveals the deep link between the golden ratio and the Fibonacci sequence.

F_n.description: The nth term of the sequence.

\\varphi.description: (1+root 5)/2, about 1.618. It is the positive characteristic root.

\\psi.description: (1-root 5)/2, about -0.618. It is the negative characteristic root.

\\sqrt{5}.description: The difference between the two characteristic roots; dividing by it makes the result an integer.

n.description: The position in the Fibonacci sequence you want.

realWorldExamples: Computing the performance bounds of a Fibonacci heap in algorithm analysis
Explaining golden ratio patterns in nature, such as petal counts and pine cone spirals
Deriving Fibonacci retracement levels in finance
